lead: A crystallizer turns dissolved solute into solid crystals by creating supersaturation and then controlling nucleation and growth. It must also remove or supply heat. The way a unit creates supersaturation names its class: cooling, evaporative/vacuum, reaction or salting-out. Yield follows a solute balance against solubility. Heat duty follows a heat balance that includes sensible cooling, evaporation and heat of crystallization. These ideas size crystallizers for sugar, salt, urea, pharmaceuticals and water treatment.
prereq: You need: solubility and supersaturation (6.5) and nucleation and growth (6.6).

sections.h3: Classification by supersaturation and heat removal

blocks.text: Every crystallizer must create supersaturation. The class name comes from how it does that. Cooling crystallizers cool the solution; solubility falls and solute crystallizes. Evaporative crystallizers boil off solvent; the solution becomes more concentrated. A vacuum crystallizer flashes solvent at low pressure, so evaporation removes sensible heat and causes cooling. Reaction crystallizers form a sparingly soluble product by mixing reactants. Salting-out units add a foreign substance that lowers solubility.

Operation is batch or continuous. Batch units suit small volumes, seasonal products or recipe changes. Continuous units suit large steady production and give steadier product size. The stirred tank is the simple batch cooling unit. The Swenson-Walker is a continuous cooling trough with scrapers that move crystals and keep heat-transfer surfaces clean. A forced-circulation crystallizer pumps magma through an external heat exchanger; this gives good heat transfer with low supersaturation at the crystal bed. The draft-tube-baffle unit uses an internal propeller and a baffle to suspend crystals. The Oslo crystallizer grows crystals in a fluidized bed and withdraws a classified product.

sections.h3: Yield and purity from a solute balance

blocks.text: Yield comes from the solute left dissolved in the mother liquor at the final temperature. Use solubility as mass of solute per 100 mass of water, not per 100 mass of solution. For feed F kg/h with solute mass fraction x<sub>F</sub>, solute in feed is S<sub>F</sub> = F x<sub>F</sub>. Water in feed is W = F - S<sub>F</sub>. At the final temperature, mother liquor holds S<sub>L</sub> = W s/100, where s is solubility in g solute per 100 g water. For anhydrous crystals, crystal mass P = S<sub>F</sub> - S<sub>L</sub>. Keep all masses in the same unit, usually kg/h.
P = F x<sub>F</sub> - (F - F x<sub>F</sub>) s/100 = F[x<sub>F</sub> - (1 - x<sub>F</sub>) s/100]
blocks.where: P is crystal mass flow (kg/h); F is feed mass flow (kg/h); x<sub>F</sub> is solute mass fraction in feed; s is solubility (kg solute per 100 kg water).

blocks.text: Purity differs from yield. Yield counts solute recovered. Purity counts the wanted solid as a fraction of product mass. Mother liquor film, other soluble salts and hydrate water lower purity. Washing removes the film. If crystals are a hydrate, crystal mass includes water of crystallization: P = (S<sub>F</sub> - S<sub>L</sub>)/y<sub>c</sub>, where y<sub>c</sub> is solute mass fraction in the hydrate. That water must also enter the water balance. Saturated mother liquor always carries solute, so 100% yield needs recycle or further treatment.

sections.h3: Heat effects and design of batch and continuous units

blocks.text: The heat balance depends on the crystallizer type. In a cooling crystallizer with no evaporation, heat leaves through the wall.
Q = m<sub>f</sub> c<sub>p,f</sub> (T<sub>f</sub> - T) + P ΔH<sub>c</sub>
blocks.where: Q is heat removed through the wall (kJ/h); m<sub>f</sub> is feed mass flow (kg/h); c<sub>p,f</sub> is feed specific heat (kJ/(kg K)); T<sub>f</sub> and T are initial and final temperatures (K or °C); P is crystal mass flow (kg/h); ΔH<sub>c</sub> is heat of crystallization (kJ/kg).

blocks.text: Cooling water flow is m<sub>w</sub> = Q/(c<sub>p,w</sub> ΔT<sub>w</sub>).

blocks.where: m<sub>w</sub> is cooling water flow (kg/h); c<sub>p,w</sub> is water specific heat (kJ/(kg K)); ΔT<sub>w</sub> is water temperature rise (K).

blocks.text: For an evaporative crystallizer heated by steam, steam supplies heat to raise feed to boiling, to crystallize and to evaporate solvent.
Q<sub>steam</sub> = m<sub>f</sub> c<sub>p,f</sub> (T<sub>b</sub> - T<sub>f</sub>) + P ΔH<sub>c</sub> + m<sub>v</sub> ΔH<sub>vap</sub>
blocks.where: Q<sub>steam</sub> is steam duty (kJ/h); T<sub>b</sub> is boiling temperature (K or °C); m<sub>v</sub> is evaporated solvent (kg/h); ΔH<sub>vap</sub> is latent heat of vaporization (kJ/kg); other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: For a vacuum crystallizer with no external heat, solvent flashes and carries latent heat from the liquor.
m<sub>v</sub> ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = m<sub>f</sub> c<sub>p,f</sub> (T<sub>f</sub> - T) + P ΔH<sub>c</sub>
blocks.where: m<sub>v</sub> is flashed solvent (kg/h); ΔH<sub>vap</sub> is latent heat (kJ/kg); other symbols are as above. Solve this for m<sub>v</sub>. External cooling water is small or zero.

blocks.text: Design keeps supersaturation inside the metastable zone. Too high a supersaturation gives many nuclei and fine crystals; too low gives little growth and low yield. Key variables are residence time, magma density (mass of crystals per volume of slurry), circulation rate, temperature difference across heat-transfer surfaces and heat-transfer area. Magma is the slurry of crystals in mother liquor. A cooling crystallizer needs Q = U A ΔTlm to size area, where U is overall heat-transfer coefficient (kJ/(h m² K)) and A is heat-transfer area (m²). ΔTlm is the log-mean temperature difference between the magma and the coolant, the log-mean of the two end differences. A small ΔT needs large area but gives gentler supersaturation and less encrustation. Batch design fixes the cooling curve and batch time. Continuous design fixes residence time and withdrawal rate. High-circulation units such as forced-circulation and draft-tube reduce local supersaturation. Crystal size distribution is covered in 6.8.

figure.caption: Classification by supersaturation method: cooling removes heat; evaporative (vacuum) removes solvent; reaction forms a sparingly soluble product; salting-out adds a salt that lowers solubility. Notes give common examples.

spec.aria: A classification tree of crystallizers into cooling, evaporative, reaction and salting-out types, with common examples in each note.

examples.question: A feed of 1000 kg/h contains 30 mass% solute at 50 °C and is cooled to 20 °C. Solubility at 20 °C is 20 g solute per 100 g water. The feed solution has c<sub>p</sub> = 3.8 kJ/(kg K). Heat of crystallization is 120 kJ/kg crystals. Cooling water has ΔT = 10 K and c<sub>p</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg K). Find the crystal yield and cooling water flow.
steps: At 20 °C, solubility = 20 kg solute per 100 kg water = 0.20 kg/kg water.
Dissolved solute in mother liquor S<sub>L</sub> = 700 × 0.20 = 140 kg/h.
examples.answer: Crystal yield is 160.0 kg/h and cooling water flow is 3186.6 kg/h.
examples.check:
F=1000.0
xF=0.30
Tf=50.0
T=20.0
sol=20.0/100.0
cp_f=3.8
Hc=120.0
cp_w=4.18
dTw=10.0
S_F=F*xF
W=F-S_F
S_L=W*sol
P=S_F-S_L
Q=F*cp_f*(Tf-T)
Qc=P*Hc
Qtot=Q+Qc
mw=Qtot/(cp_w*dTw)
print(round(P,1))
print(round(mw,1))

traps: Using the feed mass as water. Only 700 kg/h is water in the example; using 1000 kg/h overestimates mother-liquor solute and underestimates crystals.
Forgetting the heat of crystallization. It is released, so it adds to the cooling load.
Reading solubility as g per 100 g solution instead of g per 100 g water. The denominator is water.
Treating hydrate crystals as anhydrous. Water of crystallization changes both the crystal mass and the water balance.

quiz.q: Name two cooling crystallizers and three evaporative/vacuum crystallizers.
quiz.a: Cooling: stirred tank, Swenson-Walker. Vacuum/evaporative: vacuum crystallizer, draft-tube-baffle, forced-circulation.

quiz.q: Why does a vacuum crystallizer need little external cooling water?
quiz.a: Solvent flashes and evaporates at low pressure; the latent heat of that evaporation is taken from the liquor, so the liquor cools itself and little or no external cooling water is needed.

quiz.q: An 800 kg/h feed has 25 mass% solute. Solubility at the final temperature is 15 g/100 g water. Find anhydrous crystals.
quiz.a: Solute = 200 kg/h; water = 600 kg/h; dissolved = 90 kg/h; crystals = 110 kg/h.

quiz.q: What changes when the product is a hydrate rather than an anhydrous crystal?
quiz.a: Crystal mass includes water of crystallization; use solute fraction in the hydrate. The water balance loses water to crystals, so mother liquor water and dissolved solute fall.

quiz.q: Cooling water ΔT halves at the same heat duty. What happens to water flow?
Why can a small temperature difference across a cooling surface improve crystal size but raise cost?
quiz.a: Small ΔT lowers local supersaturation and nucleation, giving larger crystals, but needs more area and capital.

quiz.q: Why is 100% yield impossible from a simple crystallizer?
quiz.a: Mother liquor leaves saturated, so it still carries dissolved solute; recycle or further treatment is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial design combines population balances with CFD of magma circulation and heat transfer. Seeded and continuous oscillatory baffled crystallizers are used for tight crystal size distribution. Process analytical technology measures supersaturation and crystal size in-line. Search for seeded cooling crystallization, population balance modeling, and draft-tube crystallizer CFD.
